options.A: Localized purulent discharge from the nipple pore
options.B: Persistent high-grade fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius
options.C: Stony hard texture preventing any milk expression
options.D: Bilateral and symmetrical fullness

explanation: Physiological engorgement typically involves both breasts evenly as milk volume surges, whereas localized pathological issues often present unilaterally. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h2)

question: Why is it clinically challenging for a newborn to latch onto a severely engorged breast?

options.A: Engorgement triggers the release of local anesthetics that numb the infant mouth
options.B: The milk becomes too viscous for the baby to draw through the lactiferous ducts
options.C: Edema flattens the areola, making it difficult for the infant to form a deep seal
options.D: Extreme pressure causes the nipple to invert permanently into the breast tissue

explanation: Severe interstitial fluid accumulation stretches the skin and flattens the areola, preventing the baby from taking enough breast tissue into the mouth for effective feeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h2)

question: What is the most common underlying mechanical cause of sore and cracked nipples in a breastfeeding postpartum mother?

options.A: Incorrect infant latch and poor positioning
options.B: Spontaneous rupture of superficial blood vessels
options.C: Routine application of cold compresses
options.D: Excessive humidity in the postpartum ward

explanation: A shallow latch places mechanical friction directly on the sensitive nipple skin instead of distributing pressure evenly across the areola. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h3)

question: A nursing mother presents with severe, bleeding nipple fissures despite appearing to have adequate milk output. Which infant anatomical factor should the nurse assess next?

options.A: Lingual frenulum length for ankyloglossia
options.B: Primary incisor tooth eruption
options.C: Mandibular bone symmetry
options.D: Palatal arch width and depth

explanation: A tight lingual frenulum restricts tongue movement, preventing the infant from extending the tongue over the lower gum ridge, which leads directly to severe nipple trauma. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h3)

question: Which clinical feature primarily distinguishes a blocked milk duct from early acute mastitis?

options.A: Inability to express any milk from either breast
options.B: Presence of purulent discharge directly from the nipple
options.C: Absence of systemic fever and generalized malaise
options.D: Permanent structural inversion of the nipple

explanation: Blocked ducts cause localized discomfort and a firm lump without systemic infection signs like high fever, chills, or body aches. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h4)

question: A postpartum client has a painful, blocked milk duct located in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. How should the nurse advise her to position the baby for the next feeding?

options.A: Traditional cradle hold with the baby head resting in the left arm crook
options.B: Football hold with the infant chin directed toward the upper outer quadrant
options.C: Upright upright koala hold facing outward away from the mother chest
options.D: Side-lying position with the baby positioned parallel to the mother back

explanation: Directing the infant chin toward the mass optimizes mechanical drainage of the specific obstructed ductal segment. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h4)

question: What is the most frequent bacterial pathogen responsible for infectious puerperal mastitis?

options.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.B: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Staphylococcus aureus, often originating from the infant's skin or the mother's skin flora, is the primary causative organism in bacterial mastitis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h5)

question: Why is abrupt cessation of breastfeeding strongly discouraged when a mother is diagnosed with acute mastitis?

options.A: The infant will automatically reject milk produced by an inflamed breast
options.B: Sudden weaning causes irreversible closure of the lactiferous ducts
options.C: Stopping milk removal worsens stasis and increases the likelihood of abscess formation
options.D: Antibiotics cannot be secreted into the milk if glandular activity ceases

explanation: Continued drainage is essential to clear bacteria and milk, whereas stopping abruptly exacerbates congestion and promotes abscess development. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h5)

question: What physical examination finding is most indicative that mastitis has progressed to a breast abscess?

options.A: Bilateral and symmetrical engorgement of both breasts
options.B: Permanent retraction of the nipple into the areolar bed
options.C: Fluctuance and localized fluid accumulation within the mass
options.D: Complete absence of pain upon deep palpation of the area

explanation: Fluctuance indicates the presence of liquefied pus walled off within the tissue, confirming abscess formation rather than solid inflammatory induration. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard component of immediate nursing care following surgical incision and drainage of a puerperal breast abscess?

options.A: Monitoring and recording output from surgical wound drains
options.B: Immediate permanent cessation of all lactation from both breasts
options.C: Performing sterile dressing changes according to surgical protocol
options.D: Administering prescribed analgesics prior to scheduled wound care

explanation: Lactation can typically be maintained or resumed, and total cessation is not a standard requirement solely due to a localized surgical breast procedure. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h6)

question: What primary method should a nurse recommend to maintain lactation when a mother with severe mastitis cannot temporarily nurse directly from the affected breast?

options.A: Regular manual expression or mechanical pumping
options.B: Administering high-dose estrogen supplements orally
options.C: Completely discontinuing all fluid intake to reduce volume
options.D: Applying tight binding bandages to suppress milk synthesis

explanation: Expression maintains alveolar stimulation and prevents ductal stasis while the breast tissue heals from acute inflammation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h7)

question: A mother expresses concern about feeding her infant milk from a breast currently undergoing treatment for bacterial mastitis. What is the most appropriate nursing response?

options.A: The milk should be stored separately and fed to the infant only after weaning is complete
options.B: The milk can only be used after boiling it vigorously for at least ten minutes
options.C: The milk must be discarded immediately because it contains high levels of systemic toxins
options.D: The milk is safe to consume because the infant has already been exposed to the organism and antibodies are present

explanation: Continuing milk removal is safe and therapeutic, as mastitis organisms are not harmful to a healthy term infant via the gastrointestinal tract. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h7)

question: Which preventive self-care practice is most effective in stopping early milk stasis from progressing to acute mastitis?

options.A: Frequent and thorough emptying of the affected breast
options.B: Restricting oral fluid intake to decrease total milk volume
options.C: Applying continuous ice packs for 48 hours straight
options.D: Wearing tight compression garments to immobilize tissue

explanation: Clearing stagnant milk relieves ductal pressure and removes the growth medium required for bacterial multiplication. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h8)

question: Why is maternal fatigue considered a significant contributing risk factor for the development of puerperal mastitis?

options.A: Sleep deprivation causes an immediate and permanent shutdown of the anterior pituitary gland
options.B: Fatigue directly alters the biochemical composition of colostrum and early milk
options.C: Exhaustion compromises immune resilience and leads to laxity in proper feeding and latch techniques
options.D: Tired mothers produce milk with a higher viscosity that clogs the lactiferous ducts

explanation: Physical fatigue lowers the body's resistance to infection and often results in hurried or poor infant positioning, increasing the risk of nipple trauma and milk stasis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T025#GNS226_U3_T025_h8)

question: Gestational age range defining preterm labour is between 20 and...

options.A: 38 completed weeks
options.B: 40 completed weeks
options.C: 42 completed weeks
options.D: 36 completed weeks

explanation: Preterm labour specifically occurs before the completion of 37 weeks of gestation, making 36 completed weeks the upper limit. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h1)

question: What primary finding distinguishes true active preterm labour from threatened preterm labour?

options.A: Presence of mild contractions
options.B: Spontaneous rupture of membranes
options.C: Elevated maternal heart rate
options.D: Progressive cervical change

explanation: True labour requires both contractions and measurable cervical effacement or dilation, whereas threatened labour presents with contractions alone without cervical modification. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h1)

question: Which ascending infection is most commonly associated with triggering preterm labour pathways?

options.A: Herpes simplex
options.B: Bacterial vaginosis
options.C: Candida albicans
options.D: Cytomegalovirus

explanation: Bacterial vaginosis introduces inflammatory mediators into the intrauterine environment, which directly stimulate local prostaglandin synthesis and uterine contractions. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h2)

question: A multiparous woman at 28 weeks gestation carrying triplets is at highest risk for preterm labour primarily due to which factor?

options.A: Gestational diabetes
options.B: Uterine overdistension
options.C: Cervical insufficiency
options.D: Placental abruption

explanation: Multi-fetal pregnancies drastically stretch the myometrium, activating mechanical stretch pathways that prompt early labour initiation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h2)

question: What is the primary role of increased prostaglandin synthesis during the initiation of preterm labour?

options.A: Inhibition of fetal adrenal gland activity
options.B: Cervical softening and myometrial contraction
options.C: Reduction of intrauterine inflammatory cytokines
options.D: Enhancement of placental progesterone production

explanation: Prostaglandins act locally to promote cervical ripening and stimulate smooth muscle contractions in the myometrium. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h3)

question: The physiological phenomenon where myometrial cells become unresponsive to the relaxing effects of progesterone is known as functional...

options.A: cortisol exhaustion
options.B: estrogen clearance
options.C: oxytocin suppression
options.D: progesterone withdrawal

explanation: Functional progesterone withdrawal changes receptor sensitivity in the myometrium, allowing uterine contractions to proceed despite adequate systemic hormone levels. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h3)

question: What is the clinical significance of a negative fetal fibronectin test in a patient presenting with contractions?

options.A: It indicates that delivery within the next two weeks is highly unlikely
options.B: It confirms the presence of active chorioamnionitis
options.C: It measures the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.D: It mandates immediate emergency tocolytic therapy

explanation: Fetal fibronectin acts as a biological glue; its absence in cervicovaginal secretions carries a high negative predictive value for imminent delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h4)

question: Why are digital vaginal examinations kept to a minimum when a patient presents with suspected preterm premature rupture of membranes?

options.A: To keep the patient comfortable during assessment
options.B: To minimize the risk of introducing ascending infections
options.C: To prevent accidental fetal injury during the exam
options.D: To avoid stimulating immediate placental detachment

explanation: When membranes are compromised, vaginal examinations increase the risk of introducing bacteria into the sterile intrauterine environment. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h4)

question: What is the primary goal of administering short-term tocolytic therapy in preterm labour?

options.A: To delay delivery long enough to administer corticosteroids and transfer the patient
options.B: To permanently reverse structural changes within the uterine wall
options.C: To treat underlying maternal bacterial infections causing contractions
options.D: To completely halt labour until the expected date of confinement

explanation: Tocolytics are rarely used to stop labour long-term; their main utility is buying a brief 48-hour window for fetal lung maturation and safe tertiary referral. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h5)

question: A midwife is monitoring a client receiving nifedipine for tocolysis. Which adverse effect requires immediate clinical attention?

options.A: Increased fetal movement counts
options.B: Mild transient maternal drowsiness
options.C: Slight elevation in temperature
options.D: Marked maternal hypotension

explanation: Nifedipine causes systemic vasodilation, which can lead to significant drops in maternal blood pressure that compromise uteroplacental perfusion. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h5)

question: Antenatal corticosteroids improve neonatal survival primarily by promoting the production of which substance?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Amniotic fluid volume
options.C: Pulmonary surfactant
options.D: Thyroid hormones

explanation: Corticosteroids accelerate the maturation of alveolar cells, boosting surfactant production to prevent alveolar collapse and respiratory distress syndrome. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h6)

question: When do antenatal corticosteroids achieve their optimal therapeutic benefit for the neonate?

options.A: Precisely two weeks after the final dose is administered
options.B: Immediately within the first hour following the initial injection
options.C: Only if delivery occurs prior to completing the second dose
options.D: Between 24 hours and 7 days after the initiation of treatment

explanation: The biochemical changes required for sufficient surfactant synthesis take at least 24 hours to develop fully, with maximal protective effects seen within the first week. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h6)

question: Why is caesarean delivery often favored for extremely low birth weight breech presentations?

options.A: To accelerate the onset of lactogenesis after birth
options.B: To eliminate the need for intrapartum fetal heart monitoring
options.C: To prevent maternal postpartum hemorrhage entirely
options.D: To prevent head entrapment and reduce birth trauma

explanation: An incompletely dilated cervix can trap the unmolded, fragile preterm head during a vaginal breech delivery, making caesarean section safer. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h7)

question: Who must be present at the delivery suite during the birth of a preterm infant?

options.A: A hospital administrator for immediate documentation
options.B: A surgical consultant specializing in maternal cardiology
options.C: A pediatrician or neonatologist for immediate resuscitation
options.D: An anesthetic nurse specializing in regional blocks

explanation: Premature infants frequently require specialized immediate resuscitation, necessitating the presence of neonatal care experts at birth. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h7)

question: Bleeding into the germinal matrix of the brain in a preterm neonate is referred to as...

options.A: respiratory distress syndrome
options.B: intraventricular hemorrhage
options.C: retinopathy of prematurity
options.D: necrotizing enterocolitis

explanation: The subependymal germinal matrix in preterm infants is exceptionally fragile and prone to bleeding, resulting in intraventricular hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h8)

question: Which complication involves ischemic injury to the bowel mucosa in premature infants?

options.A: Persistent ductus arteriosus
options.B: Respiratory distress syndrome
options.C: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
options.D: Necrotizing enterocolitis

explanation: Necrotizing enterocolitis is a severe gastrointestinal condition characterized by inflammation and necrosis of the bowel wall, often linked to ischemia and early feeding. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h8)

question: What is the primary rationale for maintaining a quiet, low-stress environment for a patient in preterm labour?

options.A: To prepare the delivery room for sterile surgical procedures
options.B: To prevent the development of postpartum depression
options.C: To minimize anxiety that can trigger stress hormones and uterine activity
options.D: To encourage spontaneous rupture of membranes

explanation: High maternal stress releases catecholamines that can exacerbate uterine contractions, making a calm environment a therapeutic intervention. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h9)

question: A mother who has just delivered a very low birth weight infant at 28 weeks expresses severe guilt about her labour starting early. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Provide empathetic listening and reassure her while explaining the complex medical triggers
options.B: Focus strictly on charting vital signs and documenting intake and output records
options.C: Inform her that preterm labour is almost always caused by improper maternal nutrition
options.D: Advise her to avoid visiting the neonatal unit until she feels completely emotionally stable

explanation: Emotional support, active listening, and gentle education help alleviate unwarranted guilt and foster coping during neonatal separation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T001#GNS226_U4_T001_h9)

question: What primary domains does maternal distress encompass during the intrapartum period?

options.A: Cardiac and respiratory arrest states
options.B: Neurological and endocrine dysfunction
options.C: Physical and psychological exhaustion
options.D: Musculoskeletal and renal failure

explanation: Maternal distress involves both the physical strain on the body and the psychological burden experienced during labour. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h1)

question: Why is early recognition of maternal distress particularly challenging in busy clinical environments?

options.A: Patients routinely hide their symptoms from healthcare staff
options.B: Subtle cues of exhaustion are easily missed amidst routine tasks
options.C: Vital signs always remain entirely normal during early distress
options.D: Standard maternity charts do not include pain assessment

explanation: High workloads and staff shortages can lead to subtle signs of psychological and physical wear being overlooked. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h1)

question: The excessive release of which hormones during prolonged labour drives peripheral vasoconstriction?

options.A: Prostaglandins
options.B: Catecholamines
options.C: Estrogens
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Stress and pain trigger catecholamines like adrenaline, causing vasoconstriction and reduced blood flow. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h2)

question: How does severe maternal dehydration and ketosis directly impact the progress of labour?

options.A: They cause immediate hyper-stimulation of the fetal thyroid gland
options.B: They instantly halt all production of endogenous prostaglandins
options.C: They compound physical exhaustion and contribute to metabolic acidosis
options.D: They permanently block the reception of oxytocin at receptor sites

explanation: Lack of hydration and energy reserves leads to ketone production, worsening fatigue and metabolic stability. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h2)

question: What is a primary physical driver of intrapartum maternal distress?

options.A: Mild gestational hypertension
options.B: Routine administration of IV fluids
options.C: Prolonged or obstructed labour
options.D: Early spontaneous rupture of membranes

explanation: Obstructed or prolonged labour places immense physical and metabolic strain on the mother's body. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h3)

question: Which of the following environmental factors commonly contributes to psychological distress in maternity wards?

options.A: Impersonal settings and language barriers
options.B: Frequent inclusion in birthing decisions
options.C: Over-abundance of privacy and quiet spaces
options.D: Excessive availability of continuous support

explanation: Unfamiliar, impersonal environments coupled with communication barriers heighten fear and anxiety during childbirth. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h3)

question: Which physical finding is a classic indicator of physiological and emotional stress in a labouring woman?

options.A: Marked hypothermia
options.B: Hyperactive bowel sounds
options.C: Persistent maternal tachycardia
options.D: Bradycardia below 50 beats per minute

explanation: Stress and catecholamines stimulate the cardiovascular system, leading to an elevated heart rate. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h4)

question: A parturient suddenly exhibits profound apathy and withdrawal after hours of intense contractions. What does this behavioral shift likely indicate?

options.A: Advanced exhaustion and potential coping failure
options.B: The immediate cessation of all uterine activity
options.C: Normal transition into the second stage of labour
options.D: A successful psychological adjustment to pain

explanation: Sudden withdrawal or apathy often points to severe fatigue and depletion of coping reserves rather than normal progression. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h4)

question: What is the clinical purpose of performing urinalysis during prolonged labour?

options.A: To diagnose immediate cephalopelvic disproportion
options.B: To calculate the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.C: To detect dehydration and starvation ketosis
options.D: To measure precise fetal oxygen saturation levels

explanation: Ketones in the urine indicate that the body is breaking down fat for energy due to inadequate caloric intake and severe physical stress. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h5)

question: A laboring patient shows signs of distress with erratic contractions and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate initial nursing assessment action?

options.A: Prepare the operating theatre immediately for a primary caesarean section
options.B: Evaluate both maternal vital signs and fetal heart rate patterns
options.C: Administer general anesthesia to halt all perceived uterine pain
options.D: Discharge the patient home for rest if cervical dilation is under four centimeters

explanation: Comprehensive assessment must evaluate both mother and fetus, as maternal distress often impacts fetal oxygenation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h5)

question: What is a proven non-pharmacological nursing intervention to reduce anxiety and fear during labour?

options.A: Enforcing absolute bed rest in a supine position
options.B: Providing continuous labor support
options.C: Strict isolation from family members
options.D: Restricting all oral fluid intake

explanation: Continuous presence and support from a dedicated caregiver significantly lower maternal anxiety and improve birth outcomes. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h6)

question: Why is encouraging frequent position changes beneficial for a distressed labouring woman?

options.A: It optimizes uteroplacental perfusion and relieves pressure points
options.B: It completely stops the progression of cervical dilation
options.C: It replaces the need for monitoring maternal blood pressure
options.D: It induces immediate uterine hyper-stimulation

explanation: Changing positions prevents vena caval compression, enhances blood flow, and helps manage pain effectively. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h6)

question: What type of regional anesthesia is frequently used to break the catecholamine surge in severe labour distress?

options.A: Epidural analgesia
options.B: General anesthesia
options.C: Spinal tap block
options.D: Local pudendal infiltration

explanation: Epidural analgesia provides effective pain relief, reducing the stress response and allowing the mother to rest. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h7)

question: Which medical action is indicated if maternal distress is accompanied by severe dehydration and starvation ketosis?

options.A: Delaying hydration until after spontaneous delivery
options.B: Initiating intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.C: Withdrawing all forms of nutritional support
options.D: Prescribing oral diuretics to reduce swelling

explanation: IV fluids restore circulating volume, correct electrolyte imbalances, and clear ketones accumulated from physical exhaustion. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h7)

question: Severe unmanaged physical exhaustion during labour is a major risk factor for which postpartum complication?

options.A: Postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony
options.B: Immediate postpartum hypertension crisis
options.C: Chronic gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: Permanent bilateral visual impairment

explanation: An exhausted myometrium often fails to contract effectively after delivery, leading to postpartum hemorrhage from atony. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h8)

question: Which of the following practices is key to preventing birth-related psychological trauma and distress?

options.A: Routinely separating mother and baby immediately after birth
options.B: Providing respectful maternity care and birth preparedness education
options.C: Discouraging mothers from asking questions about their labour plan
options.D: Avoiding all forms of pain relief during the active phase

explanation: Education during antenatal visits and respectful, compassionate intrapartum care build trust and reduce fear and trauma. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T002#GNS226_U4_T002_h8)

question: What is the alternative clinical term for foetal distress?

options.A: Placental abruption syndrome
options.B: Chronic gestational hypoxia
options.C: Uterine hyperstimulation state
options.D: Non-reassuring foetal status

explanation: Modern obstetric terminology prefers non-reassuring foetal status to accurately describe the uncertain nature of foetal well-being during labor. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h1)

question: What is the primary underlying physiological failure in foetal distress?

options.A: Premature closure of the ductus venosus
options.B: Rapid depletion of maternal calcium stores
options.C: Excessive production of maternal thyroid hormones
options.D: Inadequate oxygen transfer across the placenta

explanation: Foetal distress fundamentally stems from a breakdown in gas exchange, leading to hypoxia and metabolic acidosis. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h1)

question: Which factor is classified as a placental cause of intrauterine hypoxia?

options.A: Excessive oxytocin infusion
options.B: True knot of the cord
options.C: Maternal hypotension
options.D: Placental abruption

explanation: Placental abruption physically separates the placenta from the uterine wall, directly interrupting maternal-foetal exchange. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h2)

question: Why does the foetus pass meconium into the amniotic fluid during hypoxic episodes?

options.A: The liver accelerates bile production to clear metabolic toxins
options.B: The foetus experiences direct gastrointestinal infection from the mother
options.C: Bowel relaxation occurs due to blood redistribution away from the gut
options.D: Pancreatic enzymes become hyperactive in low oxygen environments

explanation: During hypoxia, selective vasoconstriction deprives the gastrointestinal tract of blood flow, leading to sphincter relaxation and meconium release. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h2)

question: Which foetal heart rate finding is most characteristically associated with uteroplacental insufficiency?

options.A: Persistent baseline tachycardia
options.B: Late decelerations
options.C: Early decelerations
options.D: Normal baseline variability

explanation: Late decelerations mirror uterine contractions but start late and recover slowly, indicating myocardial hypoxia from reduced placental blood flow. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h3)

question: What does the presence of thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid primarily indicate?

options.A: The foetus has experienced recent hypoxic stress
options.B: The pregnancy has exceeded 42 completed weeks
options.C: The foetus is passing normal vernix caseosa into the fluid
options.D: The mother has developed gestational diabetes mellitus

explanation: Hypoxia causes vagal stimulation and gut ischemia, prompting the foetus to pass meconium into the amniotic sac. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h3)

question: What is the primary function of Cardiotocography (CTG) during labor?

options.A: Direct measurement of maternal systemic blood pressure
options.B: Evaluation of maternal renal clearance and electrolyte balance
options.C: Estimation of total amniotic fluid volume in the uterus
options.D: Continuous tracking of foetal heart rate and uterine contractions

explanation: CTG combines an ultrasound transducer to monitor the foetal heart rate with a tocodynamometer to measure uterine contractions simultaneously. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h4)

question: Which diagnostic parameter evaluated on a CTG tracing is considered the most reliable indicator of foetal well-being?

options.A: Frequency of early decelerations
options.B: Number of maternal contractions
options.C: Exact time of membrane rupture
options.D: Baseline variability

explanation: Normal baseline variability reflects an intact, functioning central nervous system and healthy cardiac reserve. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h4)

question: A patient in the first stage of labor exhibits repetitive late decelerations on the CTG monitor and an oxytocin infusion is running. What is the priority nursing action?

options.A: Administer a dose of sublingual nifedipine
options.B: Prepare the patient for an immediate episiotomy
options.C: Discontinue the oxytocin infusion immediately
options.D: Encourage the patient to push with every contraction

explanation: Stopping oxytocin removes the stimulus for uterine hyperstimulation, which is a frequent and reversible cause of uteroplacental insufficiency. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h5)

question: Why is placing a laboring patient in the left lateral position effective during foetal distress?

options.A: It relieves compression of the inferior vena cava and aorta by the uterus
options.B: It prevents premature rupture of the membranes from high fluid pressure
options.C: It increases the rate of cervical dilation by relaxing the perineum
options.D: It directly encourages the foetus to rotate into an anterior position

explanation: Supine positioning causes the heavy uterus to compress major maternal vessels, dropping cardiac output; rolling to the left side restores blood flow. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h5)

question: What determines whether a patient with severe foetal distress undergoes operative vaginal delivery versus an emergency caesarean section?

options.A: The presence or absence of a previous abdominal scar
options.B: The maternal blood type and Rh factor status
options.C: The station of the foetal head and cervical dilation
options.D: The exact gestational age calculated at the first trimester

explanation: Operative vaginal delivery requires full cervical dilation and a low head station, whereas an emergency caesarean is chosen if delivery is distant. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT an acceptable method for immediate delivery during severe, uncorrected foetal distress at full dilation?

options.A: Expectant waiting for spontaneous vaginal delivery
options.B: Forceps-assisted operative vaginal delivery
options.C: Vacuum extractor-assisted vaginal delivery
options.D: Emergency lower segment caesarean section

explanation: Expectant management is dangerous during severe foetal distress; active surgical or instrumental intervention is required to prevent foetal damage. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h6)

question: What is a well-known major neurological complication that can arise from severe, prolonged intrapartum hypoxia?

options.A: Cerebral palsy
options.B: Juvenile diabetes mellitus
options.C: Congenital heart murmurs
options.D: Essential hypertension

explanation: Prolonged oxygen deprivation to the developing brain can result in permanent neurological damage, frequently manifesting as cerebral palsy. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h7)

question: What syndrome occurs when a hypoxic foetus gasps in utero and inhales amniotic fluid contaminated with thick meconium?

options.A: Persistent pulmonary hypertension
options.B: Meconium aspiration syndrome
options.C: Respiratory distress syndrome
options.D: Transient tachypnea of the newborn

explanation: Inhaling meconium-stained fluid blocks the neonatal airway, causes chemical pneumonitis, and leads to severe respiratory distress at birth. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T003#GNS226_U4_T003_h7)

question: What defines a high-risk labour?

options.A: Any childbirth lasting longer than twenty-four hours
options.B: A delivery conducted strictly without any pharmacological agents
options.C: An obstetric process threatening maternal or fetal well-being
options.D: A delivery that requires continuous intravenous hydration

explanation: High-risk labours are specifically defined by threats to the health or survival of either the mother or the developing fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h1)

question: Why is early identification of high-risk labour critical in clinical practice?

options.A: It permits timely transfer to facilities capable of emergency care
options.B: It guarantees a completely normal spontaneous vaginal delivery
options.C: It removes the requirement for continuous fetal heart rate monitoring
options.D: It eliminates the need for any postpartum medication administration

explanation: Identifying high-risk factors early ensures patients are moved to centers equipped to handle surgical or intensive interventions. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h1)

question: What is the primary physiological consequence of uteroplacental insufficiency during labour?

options.A: Excessive amniotic fluid production
options.B: Maternal hypertension
options.C: Rapid cervical effacement
options.D: Fetal hypoxia

explanation: Insufficient blood flow through the placenta directly deprives the fetus of necessary oxygen, leading to hypoxic states. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h2)

question: A fetus presenting in an abnormal transverse lie during labour faces which primary mechanical risk?

options.A: Premature spontaneous rupture of membranes only
options.B: Rapid unassisted vaginal delivery
options.C: Obstructed labour and potential uterine rupture
options.D: Immediate umbilical cord prolapse without complications

explanation: An abnormal lie prevents engagement and descent, creating a mechanical obstruction that threatens the integrity of the uterine wall. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h2)

question: Which condition is classified as a placental abnormality rather than a medical complication?

options.A: Pregnancy-induced hypertension
options.B: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: Chronic renal failure
options.D: Placenta praevia

explanation: Placenta praevia involves abnormal implantation of the placental tissue near or over the cervical opening. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h3)

question: Why does a previous classical caesarean scar place a patient in a high-risk category during subsequent labour?

options.A: It prevents the onset of normal physiological uterine contractions
options.B: It increases the likelihood of gestational diabetes
options.C: It raises the risk of uterine rupture during strong contractions
options.D: It guarantees that the fetus will present in a breech position

explanation: Classical vertical uterine scars have a much higher rate of dehiscence and rupture when subjected to the stress of labour compared to low transverse scars. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of using cardiotocography during a high-risk labour?

options.A: To track fetal heart rate and uterine contractions
options.B: To evaluate cervical dilation and effacement rates
options.C: To measure exact maternal blood loss
options.D: To determine maternal core body temperature

explanation: Cardiotocography electronically records both the fetal heart rate pattern and uterine contraction frequency simultaneously. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h4)

question: A nurse monitoring a patient with severe pre-eclampsia in labour notes a sudden drop in urine output alongside spiking blood pressure. Which assessment should be prioritized?

options.A: Performing a digital vaginal examination for cervical dilation
options.B: Assessing fetal heart rate via cardiotocography
options.C: Testing amniotic fluid colour for meconium staining
options.D: Checking maternal hemodynamic stability and reflexes

explanation: Sudden oliguria and worsening hypertension in pre-eclampsia signal potential progression toward eclampsia or renal impairment, requiring urgent maternal evaluation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h4)

question: What does crossing the action line on a partograph indicate?

options.A: Labour is progressing faster than normal physiological limits
options.B: No further monitoring of vital signs is necessary
options.C: Immediate medical intervention or facility transfer is required
options.D: The second stage of labour has successfully concluded

explanation: The action line represents a critical threshold where active management or surgical intervention must be initiated to prevent severe complications. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h5)

question: How does the partograph assist nurses in resource-constrained clinical settings?

options.A: It provides an inexpensive visual warning system for delayed labour progress
options.B: It automatically performs emergency caesarean sections when needed
options.C: It replaces the need for measuring maternal vital signs entirely
options.D: It removes the requirement for fetal heart auscultation

explanation: The partograph is a low-cost paper tool that standardizes monitoring and highlights deviations from normal progress before they become life-threatening. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h5)

question: Why is the left lateral position frequently recommended for a high-risk labouring patient?

options.A: It prevents the spontaneous rupture of amniotic membranes
options.B: It relieves pressure on the inferior vena cava and enhances placental blood flow
options.C: It completely eliminates the sensation of labour pain
options.D: It speeds up cervical dilation through gravity

explanation: Lying on the left side prevents the gravid uterus from compressing major maternal blood vessels, ensuring optimal oxygen delivery to the fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h6)

question: What is a primary rationale for securing large-bore intravenous access in a high-risk parturient?

options.A: To monitor exact maternal core temperature changes continuously
options.B: To facilitate rapid fluid resuscitation or blood transfusion if hemorrhage occurs
options.C: To measure internal fetal scalp pH levels directly
options.D: To allow continuous administration of oral nutritional supplements

explanation: High-risk labours carry a substantial risk of sudden severe bleeding, requiring wide-bore access to quickly replace volume and administer blood products. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h6)

question: Which physical maneuver is contraindicated when managing shoulder dystocia?

options.A: Fundal pressure
options.B: Clearing the fetal mouth
options.C: Suprapubic pressure
options.D: McRoberts maneuver

explanation: Pushing on the uterine fundus during shoulder dystocia worsens impaction and significantly increases the risk of uterine rupture. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h7)

question: What is the immediate priority when a pregnant patient experiences an eclamptic seizure during labour?

options.A: Inserting a rigid plastic bite block between the teeth during convulsions
options.B: Ensuring a patent airway and protecting the patient from physical injury
options.C: Administering oral antihypertensive medications immediately
options.D: Performing an immediate emergency forceps delivery in the labour ward bed

explanation: Patient safety and airway preservation take absolute precedence during an active seizure to prevent aspiration and trauma. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h7)

question: Prolonged and obstructed labour is most directly associated with the development of which long-term condition?

options.A: Chronic essential hypertension
options.B: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: Postpartum thyroiditis
options.D: Obstetric fistula

explanation: Extended pressure from the fetal head against the pelvis cuts off blood supply, leading to tissue necrosis and the formation of fistulas between the tract and bladder or rectum. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h8)

question: Why is continued blood pressure monitoring essential in the days following a high-risk hypertensive labour?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any postnatal physical activity
options.B: Postpartum monitoring prevents the development of gestational diabetes
options.C: Blood pressure values always normalize immediately after placental delivery
options.D: Hypertension can persist or worsen in the immediate postpartum period

explanation: Women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy remain at risk for postpartum pre-eclampsia, stroke, and eclamptic seizures after delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T004#GNS226_U4_T004_h8)

question: What abnormal hemoglobin variant is primarily responsible for sickle cell disease?

options.A: Hemoglobin A
options.B: Hemoglobin F
options.C: Hemoglobin S
options.D: Hemoglobin C

explanation: Sickle cell disease is caused by a genetic mutation that produces abnormal hemoglobin S, which polymerizes under low oxygen tension. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h1)

question: Why do red blood cells assume a characteristic crescent shape in individuals with sickle cell disease?

options.A: Hemoglobin S polymerizes under low oxygen tension
options.B: Excess iron accumulation stiffens the cell membrane
options.C: Platelets adhere to the erythrocyte surface
options.D: Leukocyte infiltration destroys the cell cytoskeleton

explanation: Deoxygenation causes hemoglobin S molecules to stick together and form long rigid polymers, distorting the cell into a sickle shape. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h1)

question: By approximately what percentage does total blood volume expand during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: Seventy-five percent
options.B: Fifty percent
options.C: Ten percent
options.D: Twenty-five percent

explanation: Maternal blood volume increases substantially during pregnancy to meet the metabolic demands of the fetus and placenta, reaching up to a 50 percent expansion by the third trimester. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h2)

question: How does the normal hypercoagulable state of pregnancy interact with sickle cell disease?

options.A: It heightens the baseline risk of vascular thrombosis and organ infarction
options.B: It reduces the frequency of acute painful crises by stabilizing blood flow
options.C: It completely neutralizes the hemolytic anemia associated with hemoglobin S
options.D: It prevents red blood cell polymerization in the microvasculature

explanation: Pregnancy naturally increases clotting factors, which, combined with the sluggish blood flow from sickled cells, greatly amplifies the danger of vaso-occlusive events. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h2)

question: What is a primary cause of intrauterine growth restriction in pregnancies complicated by sickle cell disease?

options.A: Rapid maternal leukocyte destruction in the spleen
options.B: Excessive maternal weight gain and fluid overload
options.C: Elevated fetal production of abnormal hemoglobin S
options.D: Chronic uteroplacental insufficiency from microvascular infarction

explanation: Vaso-occlusion damages the placental blood vessels, reducing the supply of oxygen and nutrients delivered to the developing fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h3)

question: Which maternal complication involves pulmonary vaso-occlusion and mimics a severe chest infection?

options.A: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.B: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
options.C: Placental abruption
options.D: Acute chest syndrome

explanation: Acute chest syndrome is a life-threatening complication characterized by chest pain, fever, and pulmonary infiltrates caused by sickled cells blocking pulmonary vessels. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h3)

question: Which vitamin supplement is prescribed in high doses throughout pregnancy for women with sickle cell disease to support erythropoiesis?

options.A: Folic acid
options.B: Vitamin C
options.C: Vitamin D
options.D: Pyridoxine

explanation: Folic acid is essential for rapid cell division and is required in higher amounts due to the continuous destruction and replacement of red blood cells in hemolytic anemias. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h4)

question: A pregnant woman at twenty-eight weeks gestation with sickle cell disease attends her routine antenatal visit. Which assessment is most critical for detecting early uteroplacental compromise?

options.A: Serial ultrasound scans for fetal growth and amniotic fluid
options.B: Daily maternal weight measurement and body mass index calculation
options.C: Weekly assessment of deep tendon reflexes and visual acuity
options.D: Routine 24-hour dietary recall and caloric intake tracking

explanation: Because placental insufficiency frequently complicates sickle cell pregnancies, regular ultrasound monitoring is vital to catch fetal growth restriction early. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h4)

question: Why is hydroxyurea typically discontinued when a patient with sickle cell disease becomes pregnant?

options.A: It completely stops maternal red blood cell production
options.B: It neutralizes the beneficial effects of folic acid supplementation
options.C: It causes severe maternal hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis
options.D: It is known to have teratogenic effects on the developing fetus

explanation: Hydroxyurea carries significant risks of fetal malformations and is avoided during gestation, requiring alternative management strategies. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h5)

question: What is the primary rationale for administering malaria chemoprophylaxis to pregnant women with sickle cell disease in endemic regions?

options.A: To prevent parasite-induced hemolysis that can precipitate a painful crisis
options.B: To enhance the oxygen-carrying capacity of maternal plasma
options.C: To suppress abnormal fetal hemoglobin production in utero
options.D: To eradicate chronic bacterial infections in the urinary tract

explanation: Malaria infection causes severe red blood cell destruction and fever, which rapidly triggers dehydration and acute sickling episodes. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h5)

question: Which intervention is frequently recommended during labour to minimize pain and reduce stress-induced sickling?

options.A: Epidural analgesia
options.B: General anesthesia
options.C: Absolute bed rest
options.D: Intramuscular pethidine

explanation: Epidural analgesia effectively controls labour pain while avoiding the respiratory depression associated with systemic opioids, helping maintain optimal oxygenation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h6)

question: What is the primary danger of untreated pain and anxiety during labour in a patient with sickle cell disease?

options.A: They cause immediate maternal hypoglycemia and sudden electrolyte loss
options.B: They trigger catecholamine release that can provoke a vaso-occlusive crisis
options.C: They suppress the normal physiological expansion of plasma volume
options.D: They accelerate the rate of normal placental perfusion and oxygen delivery

explanation: Pain and anxiety elevate stress hormones like catecholamines, which cause vasoconstriction and increase the likelihood of sickling and tissue ischemia. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h6)

question: Which type of contraception is generally preferred for postpartum women with sickle cell disease?

options.A: Traditional calendar-based periodic abstinence methods
options.B: Spermicidal barrier creams used without mechanical barriers
options.C: Progestin-only or long-acting reversible contraceptives
options.D: Combined oral contraceptive pills containing high-dose estrogen

explanation: Estrogen-containing contraceptives increase the risk of blood clots, making progestin-only or non-hormonal options much safer for women with sickle cell disease. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h7)

question: Why does the immediate postpartum period present such a high risk for acute sickle cell complications?

options.A: The sudden normalization of blood volume cures the underlying anemia
options.B: Fetal hemoglobin production temporarily ceases in the mother
options.C: Placental hormones remain at high levels in the maternal circulation
options.D: Rapid fluid shifts and ongoing stress can trigger vaso-occlusive crises

explanation: The sudden loss of blood volume during delivery, combined with the stress of childbirth and potential infection, creates an ideal environment for sickling episodes. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T005#GNS226_U4_T005_h7)

question: What is the primary physiological effect of placental hormones like human placental lactogen during pregnancy?

options.A: Enhancing maternal glucose clearance
options.B: Decreasing maternal basal body temperature
options.C: Accelerating fetal pancreatic development
options.D: Inducing maternal insulin resistance

explanation: Placental hormones progressively increase insulin resistance in the mother to ensure adequate glucose is shunted toward the growing fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h1)

question: Why does gestational diabetes develop in certain pregnant women?

options.A: Their kidneys excrete glucose at an abnormally accelerated rate
options.B: Their pancreatic beta-cells fail to compensate for increased insulin resistance
options.C: Their placenta stops producing human placental lactogen entirely
options.D: Their fetal liver begins to overproduce insulin precursors

explanation: Normal pregnancies feature high insulin resistance, but diabetes manifests when the mother's pancreas cannot secrete enough extra insulin to overcome that resistance. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h1)

question: What defines pregestational diabetes mellitus in an expectant mother?

options.A: Experiencing transient glycosuria due to altered renal thresholds
options.B: Showing insulin resistance only during the immediate postpartum period
options.C: Having Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes diagnosed prior to the current pregnancy
options.D: Developing elevated blood glucose levels exclusively in the third trimester

explanation: Pregestational diabetes indicates that the metabolic condition was already present before conception, unlike gestational diabetes which arises during gestation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h2)

question: Why does pregestational diabetes carry a significantly higher risk of congenital malformations compared to gestational diabetes?

options.A: Hyperglycemia occurs during first-trimester organogenesis
options.B: Placental hormones are absent during pregestational cases
options.C: Fetal pancreatic failure occurs prior to embryonic implantation
options.D: Maternal kidneys hyper-filter glucose throughout the first trimester

explanation: Because PGDM is present before conception, high blood glucose coincides with the critical window of early embryonic organ formation, increasing malformation risks. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h2)

question: What is the primary mechanism leading to fetal macrosomia in diabetic pregnancies?

options.A: Suppression of fetal growth hormone by placental lactogen
options.B: Inadequate transfer of essential amino acids across the placenta
options.C: Fetal hyperinsulinemia driven by maternal hyperglycemia
options.D: Excessive fetal absorption of maternal red blood cells

explanation: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta and stimulates the fetus to produce large amounts of insulin, which acts as a growth factor and causes excessive fat and tissue deposition. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h3)

question: Which complication is a direct consequence of fetal macrosomia during vaginal delivery?

options.A: Transient tachypnea
options.B: Neural tube defects
options.C: Pulmonary hypoplasia
options.D: Shoulder dystocia

explanation: A baby with macrosomia is prone to having broad shoulders that can become physically impacted against the maternal pubic bone during delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h3)

question: During which gestational weeks is the standard screening for gestational diabetes mellitus typically performed?

options.A: 16 to 20 weeks
options.B: 24 to 28 weeks
options.C: 34 to 38 weeks
options.D: 8 to 12 weeks

explanation: Placental hormone concentrations peak during the late second and early third trimesters, making 24 to 28 weeks the optimal window for screening gestational diabetes. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h4)

question: What is the clinical purpose of performing serial ultrasound scans in a pregnant woman with diabetes?

options.A: To assess the rate of maternal pancreatic beta-cell regeneration
options.B: To measure direct fetal blood glucose concentrations in real time
options.C: To monitor fetal growth, estimated weight, and amniotic fluid volume
options.D: To confirm the immediate closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus

explanation: Serial ultrasounds allow clinicians to track whether the fetus is growing too rapidly due to high glucose exposure or developing complications like polyhydramnios. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h4)

question: Why is insulin considered the preferred pharmacological agent for managing diabetes in pregnancy?

options.A: It does not cross the placenta in significant amounts
options.B: It completely eliminates the risk of maternal hypoglycemia
options.C: It can be administered safely via oral tablets once daily
options.D: It actively stimulates the production of placental lactogen

explanation: Insulin is a large protein molecule that does not readily cross the placental barrier, making it safe for the fetus without inducing fetal hyperinsulinemia from the drug itself. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h5)

question: When should pharmacological therapy be initiated for a pregnant woman diagnosed with gestational diabetes?

options.A: When the mother exhibits symptoms of severe ketoacidosis
options.B: Only after the onset of active uterine contractions in the third trimester
options.C: When lifestyle and dietary measures fail to maintain target blood glucose levels
options.D: Immediately upon receiving a positive screening result at the booking clinic

explanation: Medical nutrition therapy and exercise are always the first line of defense; medications are only added if glucose targets remain unmet. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h5)

question: What is the primary objective of intrapartum glycemic control during labour in a diabetic mother?

options.A: Suppressing maternal pituitary hormone output during delivery
options.B: Preventing both maternal ketoacidosis and neonatal hypoglycemia
options.C: Preventing the premature rupture of fetal membranes
options.D: Accelerating cervical effacement and shortening the first stage of labour

explanation: Maintaining tight maternal glucose limits during labour prevents spikes that would otherwise provoke fetal hyperinsulinemia and subsequent severe neonatal blood sugar drops after birth. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h6)

question: Why are women with well-controlled pregestational diabetes often offered a scheduled delivery around 38 to 39 weeks?

options.A: To ensure the maternal pancreas has time to regenerate beta-cells
options.B: To bypass the natural surge of placental progesterone in week 40
options.C: To prevent the spontaneous onset of maternal eclampsia
options.D: To reduce the risk of late-term stillbirth and excessive macrosomia

explanation: As pregnancy extends past term, the risk of stillbirth rises in diabetic pregnancies, making timed delivery a safer option for the fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h6)

question: Why does neonatal hypoglycemia frequently occur immediately after the birth of an infant born to a diabetic mother?

options.A: The infant's pancreas continues high insulin production without maternal glucose supply
options.B: Breastmilk contains insufficient glucose to support high metabolic demands
options.C: The newborn liver loses its ability to convert glycogen into glucose
options.D: Placental hormones remain active in the newborn circulation for several days

explanation: In utero, high maternal glucose drove high fetal insulin output. Once the cord is cut, that high insulin level persists temporarily and rapidly strips glucose from the newborn's blood. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h7)

question: What happens to a mother's insulin requirements immediately following the delivery of the placenta?

options.A: They increase twofold to compensate for surgical blood loss
options.B: They drop sharply because anti-insulin placental hormones are expelled
options.C: They remain unchanged until lactation is fully established
options.D: They fluctuate wildly due to sudden postpartum thyroiditis

explanation: The placenta is the source of hormones causing insulin resistance; once delivered, the mother's insulin sensitivity returns almost immediately toward pre-pregnancy baselines. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h7)

question: When should a woman with a history of gestational diabetes undergo a postpartum glucose tolerance test to reclassify her status?

options.A: At 6 weeks postpartum
options.B: Only during her subsequent pregnancy
options.C: Within 24 hours after delivery
options.D: At 6 months postpartum

explanation: The standard clinical guideline is to perform a 75-gram OGTT around 6 weeks postpartum to confirm whether gestational glucose intolerance has resolved or progressed to overt diabetes. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h8)

question: Which of the following educational points is most critical for a pregnant client newly prescribed self-monitoring of blood glucose?

options.A: Demonstrating proper finger-prick technique and recording results accurately
options.B: Advising her to stop testing once she reaches the third trimester
options.C: Telling her to report blood glucose values only during annual clinic visits
options.D: Instructing the client to double her insulin dose if she skips a meal

explanation: Accurate self-monitoring requires proper mechanical technique and faithful record-keeping so the healthcare team can adjust management safely. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T006#GNS226_U4_T006_h8)

question: What is the typical effect of normal pregnancy on the maternal glomerular filtration rate?

options.A: It increases by up to fifty percent
options.B: It fluctuates wildly every trimester
options.C: It decreases by approximately half
options.D: It remains entirely unchanged throughout

explanation: Pregnancy triggers early and sustained renal vasodilation, driving up both renal plasma flow and the glomerular filtration rate significantly. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h1)

question: Why is physiological hydronephrosis during pregnancy more commonly observed on the right side?

options.A: Dextrorotation of the gravid uterus and the left sigmoid colon
options.B: Congenital weakness exclusive to the right ureteric wall
options.C: Compression from the liver enlarging during the second trimester
options.D: Higher urinary volume production by the right kidney alone

explanation: The pregnant uterus typically twists slightly to the right, and the sigmoid colon sits on the left side, buffering the left ureter from direct compression. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h1)

question: Chronic kidney disease diagnosed during pregnancy is clinically defined as renal impairment present before which gestational age?

options.A: Twelve weeks of gestation
options.B: Twenty weeks of gestation
options.C: Thirty-six weeks of gestation
options.D: Twenty-eight weeks of gestation

explanation: Renal dysfunction identified prior to twenty weeks is classified as pre-existing chronic kidney disease, whereas new-onset severe proteinuria or hypertension after this mark often points toward preeclampsia. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h2)

question: Which condition represents a pregnancy-specific renal complication rather than pre-existing chronic renal illness?

options.A: Preeclampsia-associated acute kidney injury
options.B: Chronic diabetic nephropathy from type 1 diabetes
options.C: Long-standing immunoglobulin A nephropathy
options.D: Polycystic kidney disease diagnosed in childhood

explanation: Preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder unique to human pregnancy that frequently targets the renal endothelium, causing sudden glomerular endotheliosis. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h2)

question: A pregnant patient with underlying chronic kidney disease is at a markedly higher risk of developing which obstetric complication?

options.A: Gestational gestational diabetes
options.B: Persistent hyperemesis gravidarum
options.C: Superimposed preeclampsia
options.D: Postpartum thyroiditis storm

explanation: Damaged renal vasculature and endothelial dysfunction predispose women with pre-existing kidney disease to develop superimposed preeclampsia later in pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h3)

question: What is a common fetal consequence associated with severe maternal renal impairment and chronic hypertension?

options.A: Intrauterine growth restriction
options.B: Macrosomia and excessive birth weight
options.C: Post-term delivery past forty-two weeks
options.D: Polyhydramnios from fetal diuresis

explanation: Inadequate uteroplacental perfusion resulting from maternal vascular disease restricts nutrient and oxygen delivery, impairing normal fetal growth. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h3)

question: What is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating suspected renal pathology during pregnancy due to safety profiles?

options.A: Intravenous pyelography
options.B: Computed tomography scan
options.C: Renal ultrasonography
options.D: Abdominal radiography

explanation: Ultrasound uses safe sound waves rather than ionizing radiation, making it the ideal diagnostic imaging choice for assessing the maternal urinary tract. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h4)

question: Which diagnostic method is most reliable for quantifying proteinuria during pregnancy compared to a single random dipstick?

options.A: Serial morning specific gravity measurements using a handheld refractometer
options.B: Spot protein-to-creatinine ratio or twenty-four-hour urine collection
options.C: Repeated catheterized specimen checks performed weekly in the ward
options.D: Immediate intravenous contrast urography to assess glomerular leakage

explanation: Quantitative tests like the spot protein-to-creatinine ratio or twenty-four-hour collection provide accurate measurements that eliminate the false-positive or false-negative results common with simple dipsticks. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h4)

question: Which class of antihypertensive medications is strictly contraindicated throughout pregnancy due to teratogenic effects on the fetal kidneys?

options.A: Selective beta-adrenergic blockers
options.B: Long-acting calcium channel blockers
options.C: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
options.D: Central alpha-2 receptor agonists

explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors disrupt normal fetal renal development, causing severe oligohydramnios, renal failure, and neonatal death. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h5)

question: A pregnant woman at twenty-eight weeks gestation with chronic kidney disease is prescribed a new blood pressure regimen. Which medication from her history should the nurse immediately question and report to the physician?

options.A: Methyldopa
options.B: Enalapril
options.C: Nifedipine
options.D: Labetalol

explanation: Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor, which is teratogenic in pregnancy and must be discontinued immediately in favor of safer agents like methyldopa or labetalol. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h5)

question: What is the primary physiological goal during the initial stabilization phase of pregnancy-related acute kidney injury caused by hemorrhage?

options.A: Administering high-dose potassium supplements
options.B: Restoring effective circulating blood volume
options.C: Restricting all oral and intravenous fluids
options.D: Inducing immediate elective cesarean delivery

explanation: Hypovolemia from hemorrhage reduces renal perfusion, making prompt fluid resuscitation vital to reverse pre-renal acute kidney injury before permanent tubular damage occurs. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h6)

question: When is renal replacement therapy such as dialysis indicated in a pregnant patient experiencing acute kidney injury?

options.A: For severe refractory hyperkalemia or pulmonary edema not responding to medication
options.B: Immediately upon the diagnosis of gestational hypertension in the third trimester
options.C: Whenever serum creatinine rises above the normal non-pregnant reference limit
options.D: As a routine prophylactic measure for all women with baseline chronic kidney disease

explanation: Dialysis in pregnancy is reserved for life-threatening complications like severe electrolyte disturbances, fluid overload with pulmonary edema, or uremia that fails medical management. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h6)

question: What is a major clinical risk if asymptomatic bacteriuria is left untreated in a pregnant patient?

options.A: Permanent postpartum ovarian failure
options.B: Development of congenital hydrocephalus
options.C: Instantaneous fetal neural tube defects
options.D: Progression to acute pyelonephritis

explanation: Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria frequently ascends the dilated ureters during pregnancy, culminating in acute pyelonephritis and systemic infection. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h7)

question: Which nursing intervention is most critical following the diagnosis of a urinary tract infection in an antenatal clinic client?

options.A: Recommending high-dose herbal infusions to alkalize the urine pH rapidly
options.B: Restricting fluid intake drastically to allow the bladder and kidneys to rest
options.C: Emphasizing completion of the entire antibiotic course even after symptoms resolve
options.D: Inserting an indwelling Foley catheter for continuous drainage throughout gestation

explanation: Ensuring medication compliance prevents treatment failure and recurrent infections that threaten both maternal and fetal health. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h7)

question: What is a primary hemodynamic risk during the immediate postpartum period for a patient with severe chronic renal disease?

options.A: Abrupt normalization of kidney function within twenty-four hours
options.B: Spontaneous resolution of all underlying hypertensive vascular damage
options.C: Pulmonary edema from sudden shifts in intravascular fluid volume
options.D: Severe chronic dehydration due to persistent excessive diuresis

explanation: The autotransfusion of uteroplacental blood into the systemic circulation after delivery can easily overload a compromised cardiovascular and renal system, triggering pulmonary edema. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h8)

question: Which postpartum assessment is especially critical for a patient with a history of renal impairment and hypertensive complications?

options.A: Continuous monitoring of core body temperature hourly
options.B: Routine fundoscopic examination of the optic disc
options.C: Frequent blood pressure and urine output monitoring
options.D: Daily measurement of head circumference and reflexes

explanation: Close tracking of blood pressure and urine output helps detect early postpartum preeclampsia, fluid overload, or declining renal function. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T007#GNS226_U4_T007_h8)

question: What is the minimum number of viable pregnancies required to classify a woman as a grand multipara?

options.A: Six or more viable pregnancies
options.B: Five or more viable pregnancies
options.C: Three or more viable pregnancies
options.D: Four or more viable pregnancies

explanation: Obstetric definition universally establishes the threshold for grand multiparity at five or more deliveries reaching the age of viability. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h1)

question: Why is grand multiparity frequently associated with advanced maternal age in clinical practice?

options.A: Cumulative time required to achieve numerous births spans decades
options.B: Fertility rates artificially spike during the perimenopausal transition
options.C: Childbearing is typically initiated later in life in these cohorts
options.D: Cultural mandates require families to delay childbearing until midlife

explanation: Achieving five or more viable pregnancies naturally takes many years, meaning mothers reach higher parities later in their reproductive lifespan. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h1)

question: What structural tissue replaces normal contractile myometrium in the repeatedly stretched uterus?

options.A: Fibrous connective tissue
options.B: Adipose fatty tissue
options.C: Calcified osseous tissue
options.D: Stratified epithelial tissue

explanation: Successive pregnancies lead to cumulative myometrial damage, resulting in the deposition of fibrous tissue that reduces contractility. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h2)

question: How does a pendulous abdominal wall directly influence fetal presentation during late pregnancy?

options.A: It accelerates cervical effacement long before the onset of true labor
options.B: It increases amniotic fluid production to dangerously high volumes
options.C: It fixes the fetal head firmly into the true pelvis prematurely
options.D: It prevents the uterine axis from aligning correctly with the pelvic inlet

explanation: Loss of abdominal muscle tone allows the uterus to fall forward, disrupting the normal downward vector of engagement and predisposing the fetus to malpresentation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h2)

question: Which placental anomaly is notably more common in grand multiparous women due to prior uterine scarring?

options.A: Succenturiate placenta
options.B: Placenta praevia
options.C: Battledore placenta
options.D: Circumvallate placenta

explanation: Damaged endometrium and myometrium from multiple prior pregnancies increase the likelihood of abnormal low implantation of the placenta. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h3)

question: A grand multiparous patient at 32 weeks gestation presents for a routine check. What underlying physiological vulnerability warrants close screening?

options.A: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
options.B: Insulin resistance leading to gestational diabetes
options.C: Rapid hyper-involution of the uterine musculature
options.D: Excessive secretion of human placental lactogen by the fetus

explanation: The metabolic strain of multiple prior pregnancies combined with advancing age increases maternal vulnerability to impaired glucose tolerance. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h3)

question: What is the most critical intrapartum emergency associated with grand multiparity and a scarred uterus?

options.A: Uterine inversion
options.B: Amniotic fluid embolism
options.C: Uterine rupture
options.D: Umbilical cord prolapse

explanation: The compromised integrity of myometrial fibers, especially in the presence of prior scars, places these women at high risk for complete uterine rupture during labor. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h4)

question: Why might the first stage of labor progress unusually quickly in a grand multiparous woman?

options.A: Cervical tissues have reduced resistance from prior stretching
options.B: The fetal head is invariably smaller than in primigravid women
options.C: Pelvic bones become permanently widened after the first delivery
options.D: Oxytocin receptors are completely absent throughout the myometrium

explanation: Previous cervical dilations leave the cervical stroma yielding and less resistant, often speeding up early dilation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h4)

question: What is the primary physiological cause of postpartum hemorrhage in grand multiparity?

options.A: Uterine subinvolution
options.B: Cervical lacerations
options.C: Coagulation factor depletion
options.D: Uterine atony

explanation: Fibrotic replacement of the myometrium prevents effective contraction and retraction of uterine muscles, causing atony and persistent bleeding from placental sites. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h5)

question: How does myometrial fibrosis directly contribute to excessive blood loss after delivery?

options.A: It causes immediate laceration of the lower uterine segment
options.B: It traps the placenta inside the upper uterine cavity permanently
options.C: It prevents the blood vessels from being compressed by muscle fibers
options.D: It stimulates excessive production of circulating local anticoagulants

explanation: Normal hemostasis relies on living muscle fibers clamping down on open spiral arterioles acting as living ligatures; fibrosis disrupts this mechanical action. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h5)

question: Which diagnostic modality is essential during the second trimester for a grand multiparous woman to check for placental anomalies?

options.A: Ultrasonography
options.B: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
options.C: Pelvic X-ray
options.D: Hysterosalpingography

explanation: Obstetric ultrasound is the primary, non-invasive standard for evaluating placental implantation site and identifying potential accreta conditions. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for reviewing past obstetric records during the initial booking visit of a grand multiparous client?

options.A: To calculate exact fetal chromosomal anomaly risks
options.B: To identify recurrent complications like hemorrhage or uterine atony
options.C: To schedule elective sterilization procedures for the first trimester
options.D: To determine the precise biological sex of the upcoming infant

explanation: Past obstetric performance serves as a strong predictor of future risk, guiding proactive care planning for known vulnerabilities. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h6)

question: What immediate intervention should a nurse perform upon admitting a grand multiparous patient in labor?

options.A: Insert a rigid metal urinary catheter
options.B: Administer prophylactic routine general anesthesia
options.C: Perform an immediate diagnostic amniotomy
options.D: Establish secure large-bore intravenous access

explanation: Because hemorrhage is a major high-probability risk, securing large-bore IV access early ensures readiness for rapid fluid and blood resuscitation. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h7)

question: Why is the administration of oxytocin for labor augmentation particularly hazardous in a grand multiparous woman?

options.A: It causes immediate detachment of a normal placenta
options.B: It can provoke hyperstimulation leading to uterine rupture
options.C: It rapidly induces severe maternal hypoglycemia
options.D: It completely paralyzes the maternal abdominal wall muscles

explanation: The fibrotic, stretched myometrium cannot tolerate excessive or unmonitored uterine contractions without a high risk of tearing. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h7)

question: How frequently should uterine tone and vital signs be assessed during the immediate two-hour postpartum recovery phase?

options.A: Every 60 minutes
options.B: Every 15 minutes
options.C: Every 5 minutes
options.D: Every 30 minutes

explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage often begins silently or rapidly in the immediate recovery window, necessitating checks every fifteen minutes. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h8)

question: What is the primary clinical objective of introducing family planning counseling before hospital discharge for a grand multiparous mother?

options.A: To prevent further pregnancies that escalate maternal health risks
options.B: To accelerate the physiological process of uterine involution
options.C: To enforce mandatory state population control policies
options.D: To guarantee complete suppression of postpartum lactation

explanation: Counseling empowers patients to protect their health by avoiding subsequent high-risk pregnancies once their desired family size is reached. [learn more](GNS226_U4_T008#GNS226_U4_T008_h8)

question: What hemoglobin level tells us a woman has anaemia during labor?

options.A: Below 14.5 g/dL
options.B: Below 11.0 g/dL
options.C: Below 12.5 g/dL
options.D: Below 10.0 g/dL

explanation: Great to know! The WHO sets 11.0 g/dL as the cutoff for pregnant and laboring women. You've got this!

question: Why is mild to moderate anaemia during delivery considered a serious clinical emergency?

options.A: Normal blood loss during labor can quickly push her into life-threatening shock.
options.B: It guarantees the baby will have birth defects.
options.C: It automatically stops the first stage of labor.
options.D: It stops the placenta from coming out properly.

explanation: Spotting this early is key! When a mother starts with low blood levels, even normal delivery bleeding can become dangerous very fast.

question: What primary change in the maternal circulatory system causes physiological hemodilution during pregnancy?

options.A: Red blood cell production completely stops during the third trimester
options.B: Blood vessels shrink in diameter to speed up flow
